Hospital Course:

The patient was admitted to the surgical ward for elective right hemicolectomy due to the presence of a colon adenocarcinoma. The surgery was performed successfully on May 14, 2020, with laparoscopic right hemicolectomy and side-to-side extracorporeal ileocolonic anastomosis. The patient was stable in the initial postoperative days, despite a gradually dropping hemoglobin. She briefly experienced some bleeding from the anastomotic site, which presented as melena, but this was treated conservatively with a one-unit pack of red blood cells, and the patient's hemoglobin raised to 8.5 g/dl. After four days of hospitalization, the patient was discharged with a full diet and regular bowel motion.
Discharge Diagnosis: [diagnosis section withheld]
Condition on Discharge:
The patient's condition on discharge was stable, with no complications or obstacles to returning to her usual state of health. The patient was advised to continue with follow-up care and monitoring by her primary care provider.

Instructions at Discharge:
The patient was instructed to contact her primary care provider to schedule her follow-up visits. She was also advised to obtain a computed tomography (CT) chest, abdomen, and pelvis, and to undergo tumor marker testing six months post-operation in the service of oncology follow-up.

Medications on Discharge: None

Follow-up Care: Follow-up care with the patient's primary care physician and oncologist is advised to ensure continued monitoring of her health status and to attend necessary appointments and procedures.

Hospital Course:
The patient, a 19-year-old male with no significant past medical history, presented to the emergency room with symptoms of four hours of abdominal pain and emesis. He reported undergoing a strict regimen of dieting and exercise which resulted in significant weight loss over the past months. The family member added that the symptoms started after a heavy meal ingestion.

On physical examination, the patient presented with a scaphoid abdomen, tender abdomen and diminished high-pitched bowel sounds. The laboratory workup was within normal limits. The patient stayed overnight in the ER and was managed conservatively with NPO, intravenous crystalloid rehydration, nasogastric tube, ondansetron and omeprazole. Next day reevaluation showed persistence of abdominal pain, nausea and bilious emesis. Computed tomography study revealed gastric dilatation extended to the third portion of the duodenum, suggestive of proximal small bowel obstruction. The patient was admitted for inpatient treatment.
Diagnosis: [diagnosis section withheld]
Management:
Initial management included gastric decompression by placing a nasojejunal feeding tube to alleviate symptoms of obstruction and later use for enteral nutritional support. The patient was provided with a normocaloric hyperproteic formula starting with 600 and progressed to 1500 kcal per day to reverse protein caloric malnutrition state. Additionally, psychiatry and psychology teams were consulted concerning major weight loss. The patient was diagnosed with depression and an eating disorder and was started on sertraline. The patient was discharged asymptomatic, with hyperproteic diet plus nutritional supplements and selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor.

Follow-up:
The patient's follow-ups showed weight gain and no symptoms. Psychiatry and psychology teams will follow up the patient after discharge.
label_evidence: After general surgery consultation, the patient underwent computed tomography angiography (CTA) which showed a narrow aortomesenteric angle and a distance between these structures. The patient was diagnosed with small bowel obstruction due to SMAS.

Hospital Course:
The patient was admitted following diagnosis of mucosal malignant melanoma of the hard palate. The tumor was found to have extensively spread within the hard palate with no involvement of the nasal cavity or nasopharynx, and with no neck lymph node metastasis.

Treatment:
The patient refused surgery and underwent CIR at another facility as the initial treatment, followed by concurrent chemotherapy. After one cycle of chemotherapy was stopped due to severe hematological toxicity. The patient achieved a complete response following CIR and was monitored by physical examinations, endoscopy, enhanced CT, and MRI. At 16 months after CIR, a cervical metastasis of a left jugular lymph node was detected, leading to diagnosis of stage crT0N1M0 MMMHN. The patient was treated by en bloc salvage ND with preservation of the accessory nerve, internal jugular vein, and sternocleidomastoid muscle. The duration of surgery was 132 min, and blood loss was less than 10 mL. The patient was discharged on postoperative Day 7.

Postoperative Management:
The patient experienced no Clavien-Dindo grade 3 or 4 postoperative complications. No recurrence was found by the whole-body enhanced CT performed 3 months after surgery.
Final Diagnosis: [diagnosis section withheld]
Follow-up Care:
Patient will continue to be monitored for any signs of recurrence or metastasis.

Discussions:
The patient was presented with several treatment options, including radiotherapy and systemic immunotherapy, before choosing surgery. The en bloc salvage ND with preservation of the accessory nerve, internal jugular vein, and sternocleidomastoid muscle was performed successfully, and the patient experienced no postoperative complications.
label_evidence: Pathologically confirmed mucosal malignant melanoma of the hard palate. | Diagnosis following treatment was stage crT0N1M0 MMMHN, with metastatic malignant melanoma confirmed in one of the 63 excised lymph nodes.

Hospital Course:
The patient, an 85-year-old male, was admitted to the hospital with bilateral foot swelling, decreased urine output, and a poor urinary stream. He also complained of breathlessness, anorexia, weight loss, and had a past medical history significant for anemia. Physical examination revealed multiple, nontender, firm lymph nodes in the right upper jugular, middle jugular, right and left submandibular, and multiple right-sided axillary lymph nodes. His laboratory investigations revealed findings consistent with tumor lysis syndrome, including elevated uric acid, hyperphosphatemia, and hypocalcemia. Bone marrow examination showed hypercellular smears with reduced megakaryocytes and erythropoiesis. The bone marrow differential counts revealed immature cells with monocytic differentiation and large collections of mature lymphocytes.
Diagnosis: [diagnosis section withheld]
Hospital Course:
Despite being explained about the treatment options and prognosis, the patient refused to undergo any further investigations and therapy.

Discharge Condition:
The patient was discharged home in fair condition. A follow-up plan was initiated with further medical management as an outpatient.
label_evidence: The patient's clinical presentation, peripheral blood smear, and bone marrow biopsy findings were suggestive of a dual disorder. Upon combined flow cytometry analysis, the patient had Acute Leukemia with monocytic differentiation and Chronic lymphocytic leukemia.

Discharge Summary:

Patient: 65-year-old male with multiple comorbidities including hypertension, heart failure, end-stage renal disease, and Parkinson's disease.

Hospital Course:

The patient was admitted with fever, altered mental status, and syncope while undergoing dialysis. On admission, he was tachycardic and hypotensive. The patient was empirically started on antibiotics for possible sepsis with unknown sources and was admitted to the ICU. During his stay, the patient was found to have elevated levels of troponin and was diagnosed with aortic valve vegetation with moderately severe aortic regurgitation, severe pulmonary hypertension, and endocarditis. Blood cultures grew methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus. The patient subsequently underwent aortic valve replacement and was stabilized with long-term antibiotics treatment.

Hospital Course Summary:

The patient, a 38-year-old Asian male, was admitted with dyspnea and a productive cough that was diagnosed as pneumonia with subsequent atelectasis of the right middle and lower lobes. Upon transfer to our facility, a CT scan revealed an endobronchial mass obstructing the right bronchus intermedius. After initial treatment with broad-spectrum antibiotics, a rigid bronchoscopy procedure was performed to remove the endobronchial tumor and prevent recurrence through ablation with a diode laser. Pathologically, the removed tumor was identified as bronchial myelolipoma with no evidence of hematologic disorder or endocrine abnormalities. Follow-up bronchoscopies after 3 and 12 months showed no recurrence of the tumor, and the patient's accompanying symptoms such as cough, sputum, and dyspnea improved immediately following the procedure.
Final Diagnoses: [diagnosis section withheld]
Treatment:

1. Broad-spectrum antibiotics for obstructive pneumonia.
2. Rigid bronchoscopy under general anesthesia to remove the endobronchial tumor.
3. Ablation with a diode laser to prevent recurrence.

Condition at Discharge:

The patient has shown a significant improvement in his condition since the bronchoscopy procedure and has no active symptoms related to the previously diagnosed conditions. No further treatment is required, and the patient can be discharged at this time.

Discharge Medications:

No medications are required at the time of discharge.

Follow-up Plan:

Follow-up appointments with a primary care physician are recommended to ensure adequate follow-up of the patient's condition and to monitor for any potential recurrence of bronchial myelolipoma in the future.

Hospital Course:
The patient was admitted to our facility with incidentally detected bilateral small solid renal and adrenal masses, a cystic mass at the head of the pancreas, and a paracaval mass. The patient was diagnosed with VHL disease and staged surgical approach was recommended based on the radiologic findings.
In the first stage, through a subcostal anterior transperitoneal approach, right adrenalectomy, resection of the paracaval mass, and enucleation for the 9 small solid renal masses were performed. A Whipple procedure was also performed to remove two smaller pancreatic lesions.
In the second stage, through an intercostal extraperitoneal approach, 5 pheochromocytomas were removed and 4 cystic renal cell carcinomas were enucleated.
After a followup of 1,5 years, the patient developed a left 1 cm renal mass, which was treated by percutaneous, ultrasound-guided radiofrequency ablation.
Pancreatic and adrenal functions were normal throughout the follow-up period. Blood cortisol level was 21 μg/dL upon his last control visit. There was no adrenal or extra-adrenal pheochromocytoma recurrence being detected to date.
Diagnosis: [diagnosis section withheld]
Treatment:
Surgery for right adrenalectomy, resection of the paracaval mass, enucleation of small renal masses, and Whipple procedure. Followed by surgery for removal of pheochromocytomas and enucleation of cystic renal cell carcinomas. Finally, percutaneous, ultrasound-guided radiofrequency ablation for the left renal mass. No replacement therapy was required for pancreatic and adrenal functions.

Follow-up:
The patient will be followed up regularly for the recurrence of renal masses, pheochromocytomas, and paragangliomas. Additionally, pancreatic and adrenal functions will also be monitored.

Discharge Summary:

Patient: 86-year-old female with past medical history of hypertension and NSTEMI.

Hospital Course: The patient presented with chest pressure and left-hand numbness of one-day duration. Investigations revealed thrombocytopenia, NSTEMI, and hyponatremia. She was started on IV solumedrol, a high-intensity statin, and hypertonic saline. Anti-coagulation therapy was contraindicated at this time. She was presumed to have idiopathic thrombocytopenic purpura. However, her thrombocytopenia persisted, and she experienced a rapid decline in neurologic function. She became obtunded within six hours and was intubated to protect the airway. TTP was suspected due to the patient’s declining neurologic function, and plasma exchange therapy was planned. But, the patient succumbed to cardiac arrest before any treatment could be initiated. An autopsy was performed which revealed an acute myocardial infarction.
Diagnosis: [diagnosis section withheld]
Recommendations: No recommendations available as the patient has expired.
label_evidence: The patient's final diagnosis was thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura, confirmed by ADAMTS13 assay.

DISCHARGE SUMMARY

Patient Name: [redacted]

Age: 35

Sex: Female

Chief Complaint: Dyspnea and sickle cell crisis
Diagnosis: [diagnosis section withheld]
Hospital Course: The patient presented with severe, progressive dyspnea and a sickle cell crisis. She had a history of severe tricuspid regurgitation, protein C deficiency, and recurrent deep vein thrombosis and pulmonary emboli. After examination, echocardiogram, and Doppler, a bioprosthetic tricuspid valve replacement surgery was conducted. Postoperatively, the patient had hypoxic respiratory failure requiring oxygen support, intermittent bilevel positive airway pressure ventilation, and diuresis. Twenty days after surgery, purulent secretion was noted on the sternotomy site. A CT of the thorax showed a large pericardial effusion, possibly a hemopericardium, and bilateral pleural effusions. A subxiphoid pericardial window and placement of a drainage catheter were conducted, leading to gradual improvement of her symptoms. Two months after discharge, a follow-up echocardiogram showed no pericardial effusion.

Treatment: Bioprosthetic tricuspid valve replacement surgery, oxygen support, intermittent bilevel positive airway pressure ventilation, diuresis, subxiphoid pericardial window, and placement of a drainage catheter.

Condition stabilized: Yes

Discharge Instructions: The patient is advised to follow up with her treating physicians as scheduled.
label_evidence: Severe tricuspid regurgitation, protein C deficiency, deep vein thrombosis, pulmonary emboli, pulmonary hypertension, hemopericardium
